p.src: Now, when Constable Wu turned around that day and saw the man, he threw himself down and bowed. The man was none other than Wu Song's own elder brother, Wu Dalang. When Wu Song had finished bowing, he said, "Elder Brother, it has been more than a year since I last saw you. How is it that you are here?" Wu Da said, "Second Brother, you were away so long—why did you never send me a letter? I both resented you and missed you." Wu Song said, "Elder Brother, why did you resent me and miss me?" Wu Da said, "As for resenting you: back in Qinghe County, whenever you got drunk you would fight with people and were forever embroiled in lawsuits. You kept making me wait at the yamen, and scarcely a month passed in peace; you were always causing me hardship. That is why I resented you. As for missing you: I recently took a wife, and the people of Qinghe County, having no fear of me, all came to bully us, with no one to stand up for me. When you were at home, who would have dared so much as break wind in our direction? I could no longer remain there, so I had to move here and rent a house. That is why I missed you."

p.src: Now hear this, dear reader: Wu Da and Wu Song were brothers born of the same mother. Wu Song stood eight feet tall and cut an imposing figure. From head to foot, he possessed the strength of a thousand catties and more. Had it not been so, how could he have killed that fierce tiger? Wu Dalang, by contrast, was not even five feet tall, with ugly features and a comical head. Seeing how short and stunted he was, the people of Qinghe County gave him the nickname "Three-Inch Nail, Tree-Bark Hide."

p.src: The woman smiled broadly and asked Wu Song, “How many days have you been here, brother-in-law?” Wu Song replied, “A dozen days or so.” The woman asked, “Where are you lodging?” Wu Song said, “For the time being, I am making do with lodgings at the county offices.” The woman said, “Brother-in-law, that will never do.” Wu Song said, “I am alone, so there is little to look after. There are soldiers to attend me morning and evening.” The woman said, “How could men like those possibly take proper care of you? Why not move here and live with the family? Whenever you want some broth or refreshment, I can prepare it for you myself. Surely that is better than relying on those filthy fellows. Then even if you drink nothing but a bowl of clear broth, you can do so with an easy mind.” Wu Song said, “Many thanks, sister-in-law.” The woman said, “Perhaps you have a wife elsewhere? It would be well to bring her here so you might live together.” Wu Song said, “I, Wu the Second, have never married.” The woman asked again, “How old are you?” Wu Song said, “I have idled away twenty-five years.” The woman said, “You are three years younger than I am. Where have you come from this time?” Wu Song said, “I lived in Cangzhou for over a year. I thought my elder brother was still living in Qinghe County, never imagining he had moved here.” The woman said, “It is a long story! Ever since I married your brother, he has been far too meek and let others bully him. We could no longer remain in Qinghe County, so we moved here. If we had a strong, heroic man like you with us, who would dare utter a word against us?” Wu Song said, “My elder brother has always been honest and dutiful; he is not a rough brawler like Wu the Second.” The woman laughed. “How can you turn matters upside down like that? As the saying goes, ‘Without iron in one’s bones, one cannot stand secure.’ I have always been forthright by nature, and cannot abide people who take three calls before looking back and four before turning around.” Wu Song said, “My brother is not one to stir up trouble, so you need not worry, sister-in-law.”

p.src: Wu the Elder went himself to ask Granny Wang next door for help. When everything was ready, it was all carried upstairs and set upon the table—nothing more than fish, meat, fruit, and vegetables—and warm wine was brought up at once. Wu the Elder seated his wife in the place of honor, Wu Song opposite her, and himself crosswise at the side. When all three were seated, Wu the Elder poured wine before each of them. The woman raised her cup and said, “Please do not take offense, brother-in-law. We have little with which to entertain you, but do drink this cup.” Wu Song said, “Thank you, sister-in-law. Please do not speak so.” Wu the Elder concerned himself only with pouring and warming the wine, paying no heed to anything else. The woman, all smiles, kept saying, “Brother-in-law, why will you not eat even a morsel of fish or meat?” She picked out the choicest pieces and passed them to him. Wu Song was a straightforward fellow and treated her only as his own sister-in-law. Little did he know that the woman had once been a maidservant and was practiced in flattering attentions. Wu the Elder, moreover, was meek and feeble and had no notion how to entertain a guest. After drinking several cups, the woman kept both eyes fixed upon Wu Song. Unable to bear her gaze, he merely lowered his head and paid her no such attention. After drinking a dozen or so cups that day, Wu Song rose to leave. p.src: Wu Song took leave of his brother and sister-in-law, departed Purple Stone Street, and went straight back to the county offices, where the magistrate happened to be holding court in the hall. Wu Song entered the hall and reported, “I have an elder brother who has moved to Purple Stone Street. I wish to lodge at his home while remaining ready to answer the yamen’s summons morning and evening. I dare not leave without permission and humbly await Your Honor’s command.” The magistrate said, “This is an act of brotherly devotion. How could I prevent you? You may come to the county offices each day and await orders.” Wu Song thanked him and gathered up his baggage and bedding. He had a soldier carry his newly made clothes and the articles previously bestowed upon him, then led the man to his brother’s home. When the woman saw him, she was as delighted as if she had found gold and treasure at midnight, and her face blossomed into smiles. Wu the Elder summoned a carpenter to fit out a room upstairs. He set in it a bed, a table, two stools, and a brazier. Wu Song first settled his belongings, then told the soldier to return. That night he slept at his brother and sister-in-law’s home. Early the next morning, the woman rose in haste, heated water for washing his face, and drew water for rinsing his mouth. She had Wu Song wash his face and rinse his mouth. He tied on his headcloth and went out to report for the morning roll call at the county offices. The woman said, “Come home early for your meal after roll call, brother-in-law. Do not eat elsewhere.” Wu Song said, “I shall return directly.” He went straight to the county offices, reported for roll call, waited in attendance all morning, and then returned home. The woman, her hands washed, her nails cleaned, and her person neatly arrayed, had prepared the meal, and the three members of the household ate together at one table. When Wu Song had eaten, the woman held a cup of tea in both hands and offered it to him. Wu Song said, “Having you take so much trouble for me leaves me unable to eat or sleep in peace. The county offices can assign a soldier to serve me.” The woman cried repeatedly, “Brother-in-law, why treat us like strangers? We are flesh and blood, and I am not waiting upon an outsider. Even if a soldier were assigned to serve you, that filthy wretch would be clambering all over the stove and cooking range. I cannot bear the sight of such men.” Wu Song said, “In that case, I must trouble you, sister-in-law.” Let us not belabor the tale. The neighbors pooled contributions and presented Wu Song with customary gifts, while Wu the Elder in turn prepared a return banquet. Of all this, no more need be said.

p.src: While husband and wife were still bickering at home, Wu Song appeared with a local constable carrying a shoulder pole. They went straight into the room, packed up his baggage, and headed out. Wu Da hurried after him and called, “Second Brother, why are you moving away?” Wu Song said, “Brother, do not ask. If I told you, it would only bring shame upon your shop sign. Just let me go my own way.” Wu Da dared not inquire further and let Wu Song move away. From inside, the woman muttered curses: “Good riddance! People say that when a man's own brother becomes a constable-chief, he will surely support his elder brother and sister-in-law; little do they know that he comes instead to slander and bite at us! Truly, ‘a decorative quince—fine to look at, but empty within.’ Heaven be thanked that you have moved out; at least that bane of mine is out of my sight.” Hearing his wife curse so, Wu Da had no idea what to make of it. He remained deeply unhappy and could not put the matter from his mind. After Wu Song moved into the county offices, Wu Da continued as before to carry his steamed cakes through the streets each day and sell them. He had intended to visit the county offices and speak with his brother, but his wife repeatedly and emphatically warned him not to meddle with Wu Song; thus Wu Da dared not seek him out.

p.src: In the snap of a finger, time flowed on; before anyone knew it, the snow had cleared and more than ten days had passed. Now the magistrate of the county had been in office for more than two and a half years. He had amassed a considerable amount of gold and silver and wished to send it to the Eastern Capital, there to be kept and used by his relatives while he sought promotion. But he feared it might be robbed on the road, so he needed a capable and trusted man to carry it. Suddenly he thought of Wu Song: “This is the very man to send… What a formidable hero he is!” That very day he summoned Wu Song into the yamen and said, “I have a relative living in the Eastern Capital. I wish to send him a shoulder-load of gifts, together with a letter asking after his health. I fear the roads are unsafe, and only a hero of your caliber can make the journey. Do not shrink from the hardship; make this journey for me, and when you return I shall reward you handsomely.” Wu Song replied, “Your Honor has graciously shown me favor; how could this humble man make excuses? Since you have entrusted me with the task, I shall certainly go. I myself have never been to the Eastern Capital, so I can take the opportunity to see its sights. My lord, have everything made ready tomorrow, and I shall depart.” The magistrate was delighted. He treated Wu Song to three cups of wine, but that need not detain us.

p.src: The tale now divides in two. Let us speak only of Wu Dalang, who, after Wu Song announced his departure, endured a solid three or four days of scolding from that woman. Wu Da swallowed his anger and suffered her abuse. At heart he followed only his brother’s advice: each day he made but half his usual load of steamed cakes to sell and returned before it grew late. The moment he set down his carrying pole, he removed the curtain, shut the main door, and stayed sitting at home. Seeing this, the woman grew vexed. Pointing in Wu Da’s face, she cursed, “You witless lump of filth! Never have I seen anyone bar his ill-omened door while the sun is still halfway up the sky. People will say this household has shut itself in to ward off ghosts! You heed that damned brother’s beak and are not even afraid of being laughed to scorn.” Wu Da said, “Let them laugh and say our household is warding off ghosts. My brother’s advice was sound; it saves us no end of trouble.” The woman said, “Pah! You filthy thing! You are a man, yet you will not decide for yourself and instead let another order you about.” Wu Da waved his hand. “Let it be. His words are words of gold.” For more than ten days after Wu Song’s departure, Wu Da went out late and returned early each day; as soon as he reached home, he shut the door. The woman quarreled with him several times, but after a while she grew used to it and thought nothing more of it. From then on, when the time for Wu Da’s return drew near, the woman herself first took in the curtain and shut the main door. When Wu Da saw this, he was pleased and thought, “Now this is as it should be!”

p.src: Another two or three days passed. Winter was nearly spent, and with the returning yang the weather had grown faintly warm. That day, as Wu Da was about to return, the woman, now accustomed to the routine, went to the doorway first to prop up the curtain. But fate had ordained an incident: just then a man happened to pass beside the curtain. As the old saying goes, “Without coincidence, there is no tale.” The woman had an insecure grip on the curtain pole. It slipped from her hand and fell, striking the man squarely upon his headcloth. The man stopped and was just about to flare up; but when he turned and saw a ravishingly beautiful woman, half his body melted at once. His anger flew straight off beyond the Claw-Wa Kingdom, and his face broke into a beaming smile. Knowing herself at fault, the woman folded her hands, bowed deeply in greeting, and said, “My hand slipped for a moment, sir. Pray do not take offense.” The man straightened his headcloth with one hand and bent low at the waist to return the courtesy, saying, “No harm done. Please go about your business, madam.” But Granny Wang next door had seen it all. The old woman had watched from beneath the reed blind of her tea shop, and she laughed, “Who told Your Honor to pass so close beneath these eaves? You were struck just as you deserved!” The man laughed. “No, the fault was mine. p.src: Before long, Ximen Qing came circling back into Wang Po’s teahouse and sat down inside beneath the beaded curtain. Wang Po laughed. “What a very deep bow you made just now, sir!” Ximen Qing laughed too. “Come here, godmother, and let me ask you: whose wife is that little woman next door?” Wang Po said, “She is King Yama’s younger sister and General Wudao’s daughter. Why do you ask?” Ximen Qing said, “I am speaking seriously. Stop making sport of me.” Wang Po said, “How can you not know her, sir? Her husband is the man who sells cooked food outside the county offices every day—” Ximen Qing said, “You mean she is the wife of Xu the Third, the date-cake seller?” Wang Po waved her hand. “No. If she were his, they would indeed make a fitting pair. Guess again, sir.” Ximen Qing said, “Then is she the wife of Li the Second, the Silver-Pole Peddler?” Wang Po shook her head. “No. If she were his, they too would make quite a couple.” Ximen Qing said, “Could she be the wife of Little Lu the Second, with the tattooed arms?” Wang Po laughed heartily. “No. If she were his, they too would make a fine pair. Have another guess, sir.” Ximen Qing said, “Godmother, I truly cannot guess.” Wang Po laughed aloud. “When I tell you, sir, you will have a good laugh. Her old man is none other than Wu Dalang, the griddle-cake seller on the street.” Ximen Qing stamped his foot and laughed. “Surely you do not mean Wu Dalang, the one they call ‘Three-Inch Nail, Tree-Bark Hide’?” Wang Po said, “The very man.” Hearing this, Ximen Qing cried out in dismay, “What a fine piece of mutton to have fallen into a dog’s mouth!” Wang Po said, “A grievous thing indeed. As the old saying goes: ‘A splendid steed bears a witless fool; a lovely wife lies beside a clumsy husband.’ Old Man Moon perversely delights in making such matches!” Ximen Qing said, “Godmother Wang, how much do I owe you for tea?” Wang Po said, “Not much. Let it rest awhile, and we will reckon it later.” Ximen Qing asked again, “Whom did your son go away with?” Wang Po said, “It is a sorry tale. He followed a merchant up to the Huai region and has not returned to this day. I do not even know whether he is alive or dead.” Ximen Qing said, “Why did you not have him come with me?” Wang Po smiled. “If you were kind enough to take him under your wing, sir, nothing could be better.” Ximen Qing said, “When he returns, we shall discuss it further.” After exchanging a few more idle words, he thanked her, rose, and left.

p.src: Less than four hours later, he circled back again and sat beside the curtain at the entrance to Wang Po’s shop, facing Wu Dalang’s door. After a while Wang Po came out and asked, “Would you care for a bowl of plum drink, sir?” Ximen Qing said, “Yes—make it especially tart.” Wang Po prepared a bowl of plum drink and presented it to Ximen Qing with both hands. He drank it slowly, then set the bowl and saucer on the table. Ximen Qing said, “Godmother Wang, you make an excellent plum drink. How much of it have you in the house?” Wang Po laughed. “I have made matches all my life, yet how could I have one waiting in my house?” Ximen Qing said, “I asked about plum drink, yet you speak of matchmaking. How far off the mark can you be?” Wang Po said, “I only heard you say that I made a fine match, sir, so naturally I thought you meant matchmaking.” Ximen Qing said, “Godmother, since you are a very mountain of matchmaking, arrange a match for me too and find me a good woman. I shall reward you handsomely.” Wang Po said, “Sir, if your principal wife at home were to hear of it, how could this old face of mine endure her slaps?” Ximen Qing said, “My wife is the best-natured woman alive and exceedingly tolerant. Even now I keep several women beside me at home, but not one of them pleases me. If you know of one as fine as that, choose her for me and come propose it; there will be no harm. Even a woman who has been married before will do, provided she pleases me.” Wang Po said, “There was one the other day who was quite good, but I fear you would not want her.” Ximen Qing said, “If she is good and you bring the match about, I shall certainly reward you.” Wang Po said, “She is beautiful beyond measure; only she is somewhat advanced in years.” Ximen Qing said, “A year or two either way is of no consequence. How old is she really?” Wang Po said, “The lady was born in the wuyin year, under the sign of the tiger. This New Year she turned exactly ninety-three.” Ximen Qing laughed. “Just look at this mad old crone, forever putting on that impudent face and making sport of me!” Laughing, Ximen Qing rose and left.

p.src: Now Wang Po had just opened her door and was inside the teahouse lighting the charcoal and setting the tea kettle in order. She saw that Ximen Qing, who had paced past the door several times since morning, now came straight into the tearoom; he sat beneath the bamboo blind, gazing through the curtain toward Wu Da's front door. Wang Po pretended not to see him and kept fanning the stove inside the teahouse, without coming out to ask what tea he wanted. Ximen Qing called, “Godmother, bring two bowls of tea.” Wang Po answered, “So the gentleman has come. I have hardly seen you these past few days. Please sit down.” She brewed two strong bowls of ginger tea and brought them to the table. Ximen Qing said, “Godmother, keep me company and have some tea.” Wang Po laughed aloud. “I am not the one you are really angling for.” Ximen Qing laughed too, then asked, “Godmother, what do they sell next door?” Wang Po replied, “They sell steaming-hot helou noodles, warming and exceedingly rich.” Ximen Qing laughed. “Just look at this mischievous old woman!” Wang Po laughed. “I am not being wanton; she has a lawful husband of her own.” Ximen Qing said, “Godmother, I am speaking seriously. I hear their steamed cakes are exceptionally good, and I want to order thirty or fifty. I wonder whether he is out or at home?” Wang Po said, “If you want steamed cakes, wait a while until he returns from selling them in the street and buy them then. Why trouble yourself to call at his door?” “You are right, Godmother,” said Ximen Qing. After drinking his tea and sitting a while, he rose and said, “Godmother, put it on my account.” Wang Po said, “Never mind. This old woman will be sure to write it firmly in the ledger.” Ximen Qing went away laughing.

Wang Po said, “What a rare visitor, sir! It has been so long since I saw you.” Ximen Qing laughed, took a tael of silver from his person, and handed it to Wang Po, saying, “Godmother, keep this for my tea money.” The old woman laughed. “Why would you need so much?” “Just keep it,” said Ximen Qing. The old woman rejoiced inwardly. “Here it comes—this rogue is ripe for fleecing.” She put the silver away, then said, “You look a little thirsty, sir. How about a bowl of gently simmered leaf tea?” Ximen Qing said, “Godmother, how did you guess?” The old woman said, “What is difficult about guessing that? As the old saying goes, ‘Ask no man at the door whether he thrives or fails; one look at his face will tell the tale.’ I can guess even the strangest and most mysterious affairs.” Ximen Qing said, “There is something weighing on my heart. If you can guess it, Godmother, I will give you five taels of silver.” Wang Po laughed. “I need not try three schemes and five guesses; one thought is enough to guess it perfectly. Bring your ear closer, sir. These past two days your steps have been hurried and your visits frequent. You must have your mind fixed on that person next door. Though it would never earn a place in the Temple of King Wu Cheng, it is assuredly better than Sun Wu drilling women soldiers: nine catches out of ten will succeed. Master, let me tell you: this woman was originally taken in as an adopted daughter by a wealthy household in Qinghe County, and she is wonderfully skilled with her needle. Buy a bolt of white damask, a bolt of blue silk, a bolt of white tabby, and ten ounces of fine floss, then bring them all to me. I shall go over and ask her for some tea, then say to the wench, ‘A charitable gentleman has given me cloth for a burial suit. I have come especially to borrow your almanac and ask you to choose an auspicious day for me to engage a tailor.’ If she ignores me when I say this, the whole affair ends there. But suppose she says, ‘I will make it for you,’ and will not let me call a tailor—then we have one-tenth of our chance. I shall invite her to come and sew at my house. If she says, ‘Bring it to my house and I will do it there,’ and refuses to come over, the affair ends there. But if she gladly says, ‘I will come and make it, and cut it out for you too,’ then we have two-tenths of our chance. If she agrees to come here and sew, I must prepare wine, food, and refreshments for her. On the first day, you must not come. On the second day, if she says it is inconvenient and insists on taking the work home at once, the affair ends there. But if she remains willing to work at my house as before, we have three-tenths of our chance. You must not come that day either. Around noon on the third day, dress yourself smartly and come here, using a cough as your signal. At the door you are to say, ‘Why have I not seen Godmother Wang these past few days?’ I shall come out and invite you into the room. If she rises and runs home as soon as she sees you enter, surely I cannot hold her back by force. The affair ends there. But if she sees you enter and does not stir, we have four-tenths of our chance. Once you are seated, I shall say to the wench, ‘This is the charitable gentleman who gave me the cloth. I owe him so much!’ I shall praise your many virtues, and you are to admire her needlework. If she will not join in and answer you, the affair ends there. But if she responds and speaks with you, we have five-tenths of our chance. Then I shall say, ‘How kind of this lady to oblige me by undertaking the sewing herself. How deeply I am indebted to you two benefactors—one who provides the money, and one who provides the labor. Since by happy chance this lady is here, Master, you should act as host and offer her some wine on my behalf to refresh her hands.’ You will then take out some silver and ask me to buy the refreshments. If she gets up and leaves, surely we cannot drag her back. The affair ends there. But if she remains seated, the affair will be easy to accomplish, and we have six-tenths of our chance. I shall take the silver and, as I go out, say to her, ‘May I trouble you, madam, to keep the master company for a little while?’ If she too gets up and goes home, surely I cannot prevent her. The affair ends there. But if she does not rise to leave, matters look better still, and we have seven-tenths of our chance. When I return with the food and set it on the table, I shall say, ‘Madam, put aside your work for now and have a cup of wine. It is not every day this gentleman spends so generously.’ If she refuses to eat at the same table with you and goes home, the affair ends there. But if she merely says she ought to leave without actually stirring, matters are better again, and we have eight-tenths of our chance. When the wine has warmed her and the conversation is flowing smoothly, I shall pretend that the wine has run out and ask you to buy more; you must then ask me to go and fetch it.

So I wanted to prepare my burial clothes in advance. A wealthy man nearby happened to hear me speak of it and gave me enough material for a whole set—damask, pongee, silk, and satin—together with a quantity of fine wadding. It has lain in my house for over a year, but I have been unable to have it made up. This year I feel my health failing badly, and now that an intercalary month has come round, I want to make them during these next few days; but that tailor is making difficulties, forever claiming to be busy and refusing to come. There is no describing how this has distressed me!” Hearing this, the woman replied, “I only fear my work may not please you, godmother; but if you do not disdain it, how would it be if I made them for you myself?” At these words, the old woman beamed and said, “If I could have them made by your precious hands, madam, I could die content and go to a better place. Since I have promised you, godmother, I shall certainly finish them for you. p.src: Now Granny Wang, her scheme fully laid, had lured Pan Jinlian to her house. The next day after the midday meal, Wu the Elder went out, and Granny Wang came round to invite her over. When she reached Granny Wang's room, she took out the sewing and began to stitch. Granny Wang brewed tea for her at the side, and she drank it; there is no need to dwell on this. Toward noon, the woman took out a string of a thousand cash, handed it to Granny Wang, and said, “Godmother, let you and me buy a cup of wine to drink.” Granny Wang exclaimed, “Oh! How could there be any such principle? I asked you, madam, to come here and sew for me; how could I instead make you spend your money?” The woman said, “But my foolish husband instructed me to do this. If you insist on treating me as an outsider, godmother, I shall simply take the work home, finish it there, and return it to you.” Hearing this, the old woman said repeatedly, “The good man is truly most thoughtful. Since you put it that way, madam, I shall accept it for the time being.” Afraid that her scheme might slip from her grasp, the old woman added money of her own and went to buy fine wine, good food, and rare fruits, entertaining the woman with the utmost attentiveness.

p.src: Pointing to the woman, Dame Wang said to Ximen Qing, “That bolt of satin you were kind enough to give this old woman lay here for a whole year without my managing to make it up. Now, thanks entirely to this lady's skill, it has finally been finished for me. Her needle flies like a loom, and every stitch is both fine and close. Such workmanship is rare indeed! Do have a look, sir.” Ximen Qing picked it up, examined it, and exclaimed in admiration, “Where did this lady learn such exquisite needlework? Her skill is fit for an immortal!” The woman laughed. “Please do not make sport of me, sir!” Ximen Qing asked Dame Wang, “Godmother, if I may be so bold as to ask... whose household does this lady belong to?” Dame Wang replied, “You guess, sir.” “How could I possibly guess?” said Ximen Qing. Dame Wang chuckled. “Why, she is the wife of Wu Dalang next door. That curtain pole did not hurt you the other day, did it? Surely you have not forgotten, sir?” The woman's face flushed as she said, “That day I merely let it slip by accident. Please do not hold it against me, sir.” “Think nothing of it,” said Ximen Qing. Dame Wang immediately put in, “This gentleman has always been mild and amiable. He has never borne a grudge in his life and is a thoroughly good man.” Ximen Qing said, “I did not know you the other day, madam, but now I learn that you are Wu Dalang's wife. I know Dalang as a tradesman who supports his household, doing a little business in the street. High or low, he has never made an enemy of anyone. He knows how to earn money and has an excellent temper besides. Such a man is truly rare.” “Indeed he is,” said Dame Wang. Ever since the lady married Dalang, he has complied with her every wish, whatever the matter.” The woman replied, “My clumsy husband is a man of no ability. Please do not make fun of him, sir.” “You are mistaken, madam,” said Ximen Qing. As the ancients said, ‘Gentleness is the foundation on which one builds a life; hardness and violence are the seeds of disaster.’ With a Dalang as good-hearted in his conduct as yours, ‘not a drop leaks from water ten thousand fathoms deep.’” Dame Wang, beating the drum for him, said, “Well spoken.”

p.src: Dame Wang then said, “Had you not come, sir, this old woman would not have dared go to your residence to invite you. First, this meeting was fated; second, you arrived at precisely the right moment. As the saying goes, ‘One guest should not trouble two hosts.’ You, sir, supplied the money, while this lady supplied the labor. I would not trouble you without cause, but since this lady is rarely here, perhaps you might act as host and give a little feast to wash her hands on this old woman's behalf.” Ximen Qing said, “I had not thought of that. Here is some silver.” He took out the silver, wrapped it in his handkerchief, and handed it to Dame Wang to procure wine and food. The woman said, “There is no need to put yourself to such trouble.” She said the words, yet made no move to leave. Taking the silver, Dame Wang went out. The woman still did not rise, and as the old woman left the door she added, “May I trouble you, madam, to sit with the gentleman for a while?” “Godmother, there is no need,” said the woman. Yet still she did not move. It was fate indeed, for by then both had formed intentions toward the other. That rogue Ximen Qing kept both eyes fixed upon the woman; the hussy likewise stole glances at Ximen Qing, and seeing what a handsome figure he cut, she became more than half inclined toward him. Then she lowered her head and resumed her sewing.

p.src: Ximen Qing said, “May I venture to ask how old you are, madam?” The woman replied, “I have idled away twenty-three years.” Ximen Qing said, “I am foolishly five years your elder.” The woman said, “You compare heaven with earth, sir.” Granny Wang broke in: “What an accomplished lady she is! Not only is she skilled at needlework, she is also versed in all the philosophers and schools of thought.” Ximen Qing said, “Where could anyone find such a woman? Wu Dalang is truly blessed!” Granny Wang said, “Not that this old woman wishes to gossip, but for all the many women in your household, none can compare with this lady!” Ximen Qing said, “That is just how it is—there is too much to tell! It is only that fate has been unkind to me, and I have never obtained a good one.” Granny Wang said, “Your former wife must have been a good one.” Ximen Qing said, “Say no more! Had my first wife still been alive, the household would never have been left without a mistress, like a house with its pillars overturned. Now there are any number of mouths eating at my expense, yet none of them attends to anything.” The woman asked, “If that is so, sir, how many years has it been since your wife passed away?” Ximen Qing said, “It pains me to speak of it. My first wife came from humble origins, yet she was extraordinarily clever and capable, and handled every matter for me. Alas, she died three years ago, and everything at home has since fallen into utter confusion. Why do you suppose I am always going out? Whenever I remain at home, I am driven to anger!” The old woman said, “Do not blame me for speaking frankly, sir: even your former wife did not possess Mistress Wu’s skill with the needle.” Ximen Qing said, “Indeed, even my first wife did not have this lady’s beauty and bearing.” The old woman laughed. “Sir, why have you never invited me for tea at the house you keep for your mistress on East Street?” Ximen Qing said, “You mean Zhang Xixi, the singer of slow ballads. I see that she is a wandering performer, and I do not care for her.” The old woman went on, “But you and Li Jiaojiao have been together a long while.” Ximen Qing said, “I have now taken that woman into my house. If she knew how to manage a household, I would have made her my lawful wife long ago.” Granny Wang said, “If someone just to your liking were brought to your house, would there be any obstacle?” Ximen Qing said, “Both my parents are dead. I decide for myself—who would dare utter a word against it?” Granny Wang said, “I was only joking. Where could one suddenly find someone who would suit you?” Ximen Qing said, “Why should there be none? I merely lament that my marital fate is slight, and I have never happened to meet her.”

p.src: Ximen Qing and the old woman traded remark for remark and talked for a while. Then Granny Wang said, “This is just the time for wine, but we have run out again. Do not blame this old woman for ordering you about, sir, but how would it be if we bought another flask?” Ximen Qing said, “There are about five taels of silver pieces in my handkerchief. I shall leave them all with you. Whenever we want anything, just fetch it, and you may keep whatever remains, godmother.” The old woman thanked him, rose, and glanced at the courtesan. With one cup of wine in her belly, the woman’s springtime desire had been stirred; and after all the words the two had exchanged, each knew the other’s desire. She merely lowered her head and made no move to rise. The old woman heaped smiles upon her face and said, “I shall go fetch another flask of wine, so you may have one more cup, madam. May I trouble you to keep the gentleman company for a while. Is there any wine left in the ewer? Then warm two more cups and drink them with the gentleman. I shall go all the way to that shop before the county offices for a flask of good wine, so I shall be gone a fair while.” The woman said, “There is no need.” Yet she remained seated and did not move. The old woman went out before the room, tied the door shut with a cord, then returned to sit beside the road.

p.src: Meanwhile, left alone in the room, Ximen Qing poured wine and urged the woman to drink. Then he swept his sleeve across the table and knocked the pair of chopsticks to the floor. As fate would have it, the chopsticks fell right beside the woman’s feet. Ximen Qing hastily crouched to retrieve them and saw the woman’s pair of tiny, pointed feet resting beside the chopsticks. Instead of picking up the chopsticks, Ximen Qing reached out and squeezed her embroidered shoe. The woman burst into laughter and said, “Do not make such a commotion, sir! Do you truly mean to seduce me?” Ximen Qing dropped to his knees. “I beg only that you grant this humble student his desire.” The woman took hold of Ximen Qing and drew him to his feet. Then and there, in Granny Wang’s room, the two shed their clothes and loosened their sashes, shared the pillow, and took their pleasure together. They were like mandarin ducks playing neck to neck upon the water, like luan and phoenix flying side by side through the flowers. Joyfully the joined branches grew; sweetly the true-love knot was tied. Red lips pressed close, powdered cheeks nestled aslant. Her gauze stockings drawn high, there appeared upon her shoulder the curve of a new moon; her golden hairpin slipped loose, and beside the pillow a black cloud gathered. With vows as deep as seas and firm as mountains, they sported through a thousand tender graces; bashful before clouds and shy of rain, they caressed each other into ten thousand forms of enchantment. Her warbling cries, like an oriole’s, never left his ear. Sweet saliva welled as she laughingly put forth the tip of her tongue. Her willow waist pulsed with the fullness of spring; her cherry mouth opened and closed in breathless gasps. Her starry eyes grew misty, and fine beads of sweat ran over her fragrant jade skin; her soft breasts heaved, and dewdrops trickled into the hearts of peonies. Even a wedded couple in loving harmony could hardly surpass the exquisite sweetness of this stolen tryst.

p.src: When the two had just finished their sport of clouds and rain and were about to put their clothes in order, Granny Wang suddenly pushed open the door and entered, saying, “A fine thing you two have done!” Ximen Qing and the woman were both startled. The old woman said, “Very fine, very fine! I invited you here to make clothes, not to commit adultery. If Wu Da learns of this, I shall be implicated. I had better go report it first.” She turned and made to leave. The woman caught hold of her skirt and said, “Godmother, please forgive us!” Ximen Qing said, “Godmother, lower your voice.” Granny Wang laughed. “If you want me to forgive you, you must both agree to one condition.” The woman said, “Not merely one—even if it were ten, I would obey you, godmother.” Granny Wang said, “Beginning today, you are to keep this from Wu Da, never miss your daily appointment, and never disappoint the gentleman. Then I shall let the matter rest. If you fail to come for even one day, I shall tell your Wu Da.” The woman said, “I shall do exactly as you say, godmother.” Granny Wang then said, “As for you, Master Ximen, this old woman need say no more. This excellent affair has now been brought entirely to completion. You must not break your word concerning what you promised. If you prove faithless, I shall tell Wu Da as well.” Ximen Qing said, “Set your mind at ease, godmother. I shall not break my word.” The three drank several more cups, and by then it was already afternoon. The woman rose and said, “That fellow Wu Da will soon be back, so I must return.” She slipped home through the rear door and first lowered the blind; just then Wu Da entered. Meanwhile, Granny Wang looked at Ximen Qing and said, “How was that for skill?” Ximen Qing said, “I truly owe it all to you, godmother! Once I am home, I shall fetch an ingot of silver and bring it to you. How could I deny in bad faith what I promised?” Granny Wang said, “‘My eyes await the envoy’s banners; I wait only for good news.’ Do not make this old woman ‘wait until the coffin is out before asking payment for the funeral singer.’” Ximen Qing laughed and departed; there is no more to tell of it.

p.src: On hearing this, Brother Yun thanked the uncle for his advice. The little monkey picked up his basket and went straight to Purple Stone Street. He hurried into the teahouse and found Wang Po sitting on a low stool, spinning thread. Brother Yun set down his basket, looked at Wang Po, and said, “Greetings, Godmother.” The old woman asked, “Brother Yun, what have you come here for?” Brother Yun said, “I’m looking for the great gentleman, so I can earn thirty or fifty cash to support my old father.” The old woman said, “What great gentleman?” Brother Yun said, “Godmother, you know perfectly well which one—the very man I mean.” The old woman said, “Even a great gentleman has a name, doesn’t he?” Brother Yun said, “The one whose name has two characters.” The old woman said, “What two characters?” Brother Yun said, “Godmother, you’re only teasing me. I want a word with Great Gentleman Ximen.” With that, he started toward the inner rooms. The old woman seized him and said, “You little monkey, where do you think you’re going? Every house has its outer and inner quarters.” Brother Yun said, “I’ll go into the room and find him myself.” Wang Po said, “You filthy little ape! How could there be any Great Gentleman Ximen in my house?” Brother Yun said, “Godmother, don’t keep the whole feast to yourself! Let me have a sip of the gravy too! Do you think there’s anything I don’t understand?” The old woman cursed him: “You little ape! What could you possibly understand?” Brother Yun said, “You’re just like ‘cutting vegetables with a hoof-shaped knife inside a wooden ladle’—not a drop of water can leak out, nor the smallest morsel fall to the ground. If you insist on making me say it aloud, I’m afraid the steamed-cake seller will raise a terrible scene.” Those words struck the old woman squarely in her sorest spot. Enraged, she shouted, “You filthy little ape! How dare you come farting such foul obscenities in my house!” Brother Yun said, “I may be a little ape, but you’re an old bawd!” The old woman grabbed Brother Yun and rapped him twice on the head with her knuckles. Brother Yun cried, “What are you hitting me for?” The old woman cursed, “You thieving ape! Raise your voice again and I’ll slap you right out of here!” Brother Yun said, “You old whore! I did nothing, yet you hit me!” The old woman shoved him with one hand and pummeled him with the other until she drove him out into the street, then flung his basket of snow pears after him. The basketful of snow pears scattered everywhere and rolled across the street. Unable to get the better of that vicious old bawd, the little monkey cursed and cried as he went about gathering his pears from the street. Pointing at Wang Po’s teahouse, he shouted, “You old whore, just you wait! I’m going to tell him! If I don’t make something come of this, then call me a liar!” He picked up his basket and hurried off to find that person. Indeed, after the deeds done before, misfortune now came all at once. He would overturn the grass above the foxes’ and hares’ den, and startle the mandarin ducks sleeping on the sand. Whom, after all, did Brother Yun go to find? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
